summary.title: Writing a Game Boy emulator, Cinoop
summary.one_liner: You learn how one developer built a minimalist Game Boy interpreter in C, from CPU instruction dispatch and debugging against NO$GMB through to tile rendering and ports to DS, GameCube, 3DS, PSP and PS4.
keywords: c11 anonymous structs and unions registers
emulator ports ds gamecube 3ds psp ps4
dumping tiles to compare emulator output
game boy flags zero half carry carry
takeaways: Structure the CPU with an instruction table (disassembly, operand length, handler) so one routine can fetch operands and print unimplemented instructions.
Use C11 anonymous structs and unions to access 8-bit registers and their 16-bit pairs (AF, BC, DE, HL) directly.
Debug by matching against a reference emulator, dumping VRAM tiles and comparing them with the reference's memory, and using breakpoints on PC or memory access.
Porting to other consoles required per-platform workarounds, such as caching tileset writes in RAM and copying to VRAM during VBlank on the DS, and sending input over UDP on the PS4.
summary.summary: The author describes building Cinoop, a minimalist Game Boy interpreter in C without custom mapper or sound support, as a first emulator project. The article covers register layout with anonymous unions, an instruction table that drives disassembly and unimplemented-opcode reporting, and step-by-step debugging against NO$GMB using real-time debugger breakpoints. It then walks through tile and background rendering, Tetris-specific workarounds, and ports to DS, GameCube, 3DS, Linux, PSP, PS4, and OS X via XQuartz, with notes on why the PS2 port was abandoned.
